etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English rare, from Old French rare, rere (“rare, uncommon”), from Latin rārus (“loose, spaced apart, thin, infrequent”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁- (“friable, thin”). Replaced native Middle English gesen (“rare, scarce”) (from Old English gǣsne), Middle English seld (“rare, uncommon”) (from Old English selden), and Middle English seldscene (“rare, rarely seen, infrequent”) (from Old English seldsēne).

quote.citation: 2013 May-June, David Van Tassel, Lee DeHaan, “Wild Plants to the Rescue”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 3:
quote.text: Plant breeding is always a numbers game. […] The wild species we use are rich in genetic variation, and individual plants are highly heterozygous and do not breed true. In addition, we are looking for rare alleles, so the more plants we try, the better.

quote.citation: 2017, BioWare, Mass Effect: Andromeda (Science Fiction), Redwood City: Electronic Arts, →OCLC, PC, scene: Technology: Augmentations Codex entry:
quote.text: While many material components in Andromeda are familiar, we have also discovered rarer and more valuable materials; attributable to exposure to the Scourge, or mysterious alien technology.

definitions.definition: (of a gas) Thin; of low density.

quote.text:
Sees her reflection in a butcher shop.
She finds it all quite rare
That her meat's all vanity fair.

quote.citation: 1995, George Baxter, Larry W. Smith, Mastering Magic Cards, page 116:
quote.text: Most of the time, you do this by trading low-valued rares for more valuable ones or trading uncommons for rares. Other times it's trading cards that are in print for ones that are out of print, or low-value rares for good uncommons.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From a dialectal variant of rear, from Middle English rere, from Old English hrēr, hrēre (“not thoroughly cooked, underdone, lightly boiled”), from hrēran (“to move, shake, agitate”), from Proto-Germanic *hrōzijaną (“to stir”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱroHs- (“to mix, stir, cook”). Related to Old English hrōr (“stirring, busy, active, strong, brave”). More at rear.

definitions.definition: (cooking) Particularly of meat, especially beefsteak: cooked very lightly, so the meat is still red.

quote.citation: 1717, John Dryden, “Book VIII. [The Story of Baucis and Philemon.]”, in Ovid’s Metamorphoses in Fifteen Books. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, page 285:
quote.text: Then Curds and Cream, the Flow'r of Country Fare, / And new-laid Eggs, which Baucis’ buſie Care / Turn’d by a gentle Fire, and roaſted rare.

definitions.definition: (US, intransitive) To rear, rise up, start backwards.

quote.citation: 2006, Thomas Pynchon, Against the Day, Vintage, published 2007, page 328:
quote.text: Frank pretended to rare back as if bedazzled, shielding his eyes with a forearm.

definitions.definition: (US, transitive) To rear, bring up, raise.

quote.citation: 2013, Janet Peery, What the Thunder Said: A Novella and Stories, →ISBN:
quote.text: Here I have to say that I was walking along dark-hearted, my nose out of joint about Audie's notice of her, for just as quickly as my feelings kindled, my old envy rared.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Compare rather, rath.

quote.citation: 1614–1615, Homer, “The Sixth Book of Homer’s Odysseys”, in Geo[rge] Chapman, transl., Homer’s Odysses. […], London:  […]  Rich[ard] Field [and William Jaggard], for Nathaniell Butter, published 1615, →OCLC; republished in The Odysseys of Homer, […], volume I, London: John Russell Smith, […], 1857, →OCLC, page 147, lines 420–423:
quote.text: The men, that sway / In work of those tools that so fit our state, / Are rude mechanicals, that rare and late / Work in the market-place;The spelling has been modernized.
